meaning: Lord who looks down in compassion

phonemes.desc: Short open [ɐ] with voiced labio-dental [ʋ]; the prefix ava-, 'down, upon'
Long open [oː] — lokita, 'seen, perceived, looked down upon'
Short palatal [kɪ]; the connecting vowel of the compound
Long front [eː] — the first of two long vowels the ASCII form flattens
Palatal [ɕ] like the 'sh' of 'ship,' short [ʋɐ], trilled [ɾɐ]; īśvara, 'lord'

pronunciation.approximation: 'uh-vuh-LOH-kee-TAY-shvuh-ruh' — the ś is the soft 'sh' of 'ship'; hold both long vowels; the name ends lightly.

pronunciation.note: Avalokiteśvara is Tier 1 by rule: the restoration preserves three features ASCII loses — the long ō of lōkita, the long ē of tēśvara, and the palatal ś. The Chinese translated rather than transliterated (Guanshiyin, 'Perceiver of the World's Sounds'), which is why East Asia knows him by the listening, not the Sanskrit.

domains.title: Compassion
domains.subtitle: The Lord Who Looks Down in Compassion — Bodhisattva of Mercy, Lord of the World's Cries
domains.lead: Avalokiteśvara is compassion made a person: the bodhisattva who looks down upon every cry of suffering and answers it, postponing his own Buddhahood until no being is left unsaved. From the Lotus Sūtra's Universal Gateway to Tibet's patron deity and China's beloved Guanyin, he is the most widely venerated bodhisattva in the world.

cards.name: The Universal Gateway
cards.desc: Lotus Sūtra ch. 25: whoever calls his name in fire, flood, chains, or the jaws of demons is delivered at once.

cards.name: Thousand Arms, Thousand Eyes
cards.desc: His Great Compassion form: an arm for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and saving happen together.

cards.name: Perceiver of Sounds
cards.desc: ava-lokita, 'perceived, looked down upon': his very name is an act of attention that never lifts.

cards.name: Om Mani Padme Hum
cards.desc: His mantra on the lips of half the Himalaya — the jewel in the lotus — recited for every suffering being.

symbols.name: The lotus
symbols.meaning: Purity rising unstained from the mud of samsara — the flower on which he stands above the world he refuses to leave

symbols.name: The vase of amrita
symbols.meaning: The nectar of compassion in his left hand, poured out drop by drop on the burning places of beings

symbols.name: Thousand arms with an eye in each palm
symbols.meaning: His vow rendered anatomically: a hand for every cry, an eye in every palm so that seeing and saving are one motion

symbols.name: Om Mani Padme Hum
symbols.meaning: The six-syllable mantra — 'the jewel in the lotus' — recited across Tibet, Mongolia, and the Himalaya for a thousand years

symbols.name: The blue throat of Nīlakaṇṭha
symbols.meaning: The wrathful form's throat stained blue from drinking the world's poison — compassion willing to take on even Śiva's darkest work

mythology.lead: Avalokiteśvara's mythology is a geography of mercy: the Indian lord who hears cries, the Chinese princess who gave her eyes and arms, the Tibetan ancestor of a nation, the Japanese savior of the drowning. His stories share one grammar — someone suffers, and compassion arrives already looking.

myths.title: The Lord Who Looks Down
myths.text: The name is an act of attention: ava-lokita, 'perceived, looked down upon,' joined to īśvara, 'lord' — the Lord Who Looks Down, as Monier-Williams parses the Sanskrit. The Lotus Sūtra's twenty-fifth chapter, the Universal Gateway, turns the etymology into a program: the Buddha declares that whoever calls Avalokiteśvara's name in the moment of terror — surrounded by fire, swept by flood, bound in chains, cornered by demons — will be saved, because this bodhisattva scans the world the way a parent scans a crowd for a child. Kumārajīva translated the name into Chinese as Guanshiyin, 'Perceiver of the World's Sounds,' and the translation stuck: East Asia knows him by the listening. The name is the whole doctrine — compassion is not a mood but a gaze that never lifts.

myths.title: Thirty-Three Forms for Every Kind of Suffering
myths.text: The Lotus Sūtra (ch. 25) closes its gateway chapter with a list that reads like a census of the human condition: to beings who can be saved through a Buddha's body, Avalokiteśvara appears as a Buddha; likewise as a pratyekabuddha, a śrāvaka, a king, a householder, a government official, a monk, a nun, a layman, a laywoman, a boy, a girl, a god, a nāga, a yaksha, a gandharva, an asura, a garuḍa, a kinnara, a mahoraga — the sūtra counts thirty-three bodies in all. Śāriputra asks why he is called Perceiver of Sounds, and the answer is simplicity itself: he perceives the world's sounds and responds to each. The list is the myth's meaning: suffering has no shape the bodhisattva will not borrow to reach the sufferer, and mercy wears every uniform the world issues.

myths.title: The Eyes and Arms She Gave Away
myths.text: China's most beloved Guanyin legend is also its latest — recorded in the Song-dynasty Xiangshan baojuan, the 'Precious Scroll of the Fragrant Mountain.' King Miao Zhuang's youngest daughter Miaoshan refused every suitor and every palace command, asking only to become a nun; exiled and persecuted, she held to her practice while her father's hatred hardened. When the king fell mortally ill, the diviners declared that only the eyes and arms of a person without resentment could cure him. A mountain ascetic — Miaoshan in disguise — gave them, and died; as her body was carried off, she was received into the Fragrant Mountain, revealed as Guanyin herself, with a thousand hands and an eye in every palm. The late legend gives the bodhisattva's iconography its human face: every hand is a sacrifice once made, and compassion is the scar tissue of self-giving.

myths.title: The Blue-Throated One
myths.text: Indian Buddhism borrowed even wrath from Śiva. In the seventh-century dhāraṇī sūtras — Xuanzang's translation of the Nīlakaṇṭha-dhāraṇī and the Sūtra of the Great Compassionate One of a Thousand Hands and Eyes — Avalokiteśvara takes the Destroyer's own epithet: Nīlakaṇṭha, 'blue-throated,' the one whose throat holds the poison of a churned cosmos without flinching. Here the gentle perceiver multiplies into a thousand-armed sovereign whose Great Compassion Dhāraṇī subdues demons and burns away the gravest karma, and whose wrathful faces stand at the gates of mandalas across Asia. The texts themselves show the borrowing plainly — the bodhisattva of mercy wears the destroyer's name and drinks his poison. The myth's claim is that compassion has a frightening side: it will enter any form, even terror's, to reach those only terror can move.

myths.title: The Monkey, the Demoness, and the First Tibetans
myths.text: Tibet's own creation myth, recorded in the twelfth-century Mani bka' 'bum and the treasure-texts of the Nyingma school, makes Avalokiteśvara — there called Chenrezig — the father of the entire nation. Gazing from his mountain, the bodhisattva saw that the snowy plateau was empty of beings fit for the Dharma; rays of his compassion fell upon a monkey who had withdrawn into meditation in a mountain cave and upon the rock-demoness who haunted the cliffs. Their union, blessed by the bodhisattva's light, produced six children — red-faced, hairy, the ancestors of Tibet's clans — and when the infants had nothing to eat, Chenrezig scattered barley over the snows so they could live and, in time, hear the teaching. The myth means that for Tibetans compassion is not one virtue among many: it is the literal parent of the people, and every Tibetan carries Avalokiteśvara's gaze as a birthright.

lore.syncretism: In China the lord became a lady: by the Song dynasty Guanyin was predominantly female, and her cult absorbed the island goddess Mazu and the water-and-child-bestowing Songzi Guanyin, so that the Indian bodhisattva now answers a grandmother's prayer in a Fujian dialect. Japan received Kannon, patron of the great thirty-three-temple pilgrimage circuits (Saigoku, Bandō, Chichibu) and of sacred sites like Kiyomizu, 'pure water,' where her spring still runs. Tibet made Chenrezig the patron deity of the land and the source of the Dalai Lama lineage, each holder revered as his emanation. And in seventh-century Java the Śailendra kings named themselves servants of Lokeśvara — Avalokiteśvara by his older title — carving him at Borobudur before the Sanskrit name had finished traveling. One bodhisattva, five civilizations, each certain he had been theirs all along.
lore.culturalLegacy: Avalokiteśvara is, by nearly any measure, the most venerated bodhisattva on earth. His chapter of the Lotus Sūtra is chanted as a protective rite across East Asia; his mantra turns the prayer wheels of the entire Himalaya; and the Guanyin temples of the Chinese diaspora — from Putuo Island to San Francisco — count their visitors in the tens of millions. Japan's thirty-three Kannon pilgrimage circuits are walked today as they were in the Heian period. Modern culture keeps finding him: the Dalai Lama's name is Chenrezig's in translation, and the phrase 'compassion' in contemporary mindfulness and hospice movements is, knowingly or not, Avalokiteśvara's old gaze still lowered on the suffering.
lore.extendedMeditation: Avalokiteśvara begins with an embarrassing question for the rest of us: when did you last actually look at the person suffering next to you? His name is not a compliment but a job description — the Lord Who Looks Down — and his myths anatomize the looking: the gaze that scans crowds, that multiplies arms so no cry goes unanswered, that takes the sufferer's own form as the only form that will do. In this he is Buddhism's answer to a problem the philosophers struggled with: how compassion can be both boundless and particular. His solution is attention. He does not love humanity in general; he hears one drowning sailor, one prisoner, one frightened child, and the hearing is total. The Lotus Sūtra's promise that the name itself saves is the practical corollary: anyone can borrow the gaze by borrowing the name. To recite it is to practice looking until the looking becomes involuntary — until, like the eye in the palm, seeing and reaching are a single motion.

lore.archaeology: Avalokiteśvara enters art early and never leaves: the fifth- and sixth-century cave paintings at Ajanta give him some of his oldest monumental images, compassionate bodhisattvas looming over the chaitya halls. The Library Cave at Dunhuang (sealed c. 1000, opened 1900) yielded painted banners of Guanyin among the most exquisite Buddhist paintings surviving — several now in the British Museum and Musée Guimet. At Borobudur in Java the Śailendra dynasty carved Lokeśvara into the monument's galleries in the eighth and ninth centuries, and the Kathmandu valley's Licchavi-period inscriptions invoke him by name. From Gandhāra's earliest standing bodhisattvas to the colossal Song dynasty Guanyin at Dazu, his is the longest continuous iconographic career of any Buddhist figure.
